module_title: Intellectual Property Rights: The Foundational Matrix
introduction: This foundational level introduces the concept of Intellectual Property (IP)—creations of the human mind. It breaks down the 'Big Four' pillars of the Indian IPR regime: Patents, Copyrights, Trademarks, and Geographical Indications (GIs), outlining what each protects and for how long.

core_concepts.title: What is IPR and the TRIPS Agreement?
core_concepts.description:
Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) are legal rights given to inventors and creators to protect their creations for a certain period. 
- TRIPS Agreement: The Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (1995) is an international legal agreement between all WTO member nations. India revamped its entire IPR regime (Patents Act, Copyright Act, Trademarks Act) to become TRIPS-compliant.

core_concepts.title: Patents (The Patents Act, 1970)
core_concepts.description:
Protects **Inventions** (new products or processes).
- What it protects: Functional, technical, and scientific inventions (e.g., a new chemical formula for a drug, a new smartphone battery).
- Term of Protection: **20 years** from the date of filing the application. After 20 years, it falls into the public domain and anyone can make it.

core_concepts.title: Copyright (The Copyright Act, 1957)
core_concepts.description:
Protects **Original Expressions** of ideas in literary, dramatic, musical, and artistic works.
- What it protects: Books, paintings, songs, movies, and crucially, **Computer Software (source code)**.
- Term of Protection: Generally, the **Lifetime of the author + 60 years** after their death. (For cinematography/sound recordings, it is 60 years from publication).

core_concepts.title: Trademarks (The Trade Marks Act, 1999)
core_concepts.description:
Protects **Brand Identity**.
- What it protects: Words, logos, symbols, slogans, or designs that distinguish the goods/services of one enterprise from those of others (e.g., the Nike Apple logo, the name 'Coca-Cola').
- Term of Protection: **10 years**, but it can be renewed indefinitely every 10 years. (The only IP that can technically last forever).

core_concepts.title: Geographical Indications (The GI Act, 1999)
core_concepts.description:
Protects **Regional Origin**.
- What it protects: Goods (agricultural, natural, or manufactured) that have a specific geographical origin and possess qualities or a reputation tied to that place (e.g., Darjeeling Tea, Kanchipuram Silk, Basmati Rice).
- Term of Protection: **10 years**, renewable indefinitely.

important_entities.name: The Idea-Expression Dichotomy
important_entities.key_fact: Copyright protects the expression, NEVER the idea itself.
important_entities.significance: A fundamental rule of Copyright law. If you have a brilliant idea for a movie about a boy wizard going to a magical school, you cannot copyright the *idea*. Anyone can make a movie about a boy wizard. You can only copyright your specific *expression* of it (the exact script, names like Harry Potter, specific dialogue).

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Examiners often ask to distinguish between a TM and a GI. A Trademark is owned by a specific individual or company (e.g., Tata, Apple) and distinguishes their goods. A Geographical Indication is a **collective right** owned by a community of producers in a specific region (e.g., all tea growers in Darjeeling who follow the rules can use the 'Darjeeling Tea' GI). No single company owns a GI.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Memorize these numbers, as they are the most frequently tested objective facts in CLAT and State PSCs.

exam_strategy_tips: Whenever a Judiciary question asks 'Which IP right protects computer software code?', unconditionally select **Copyright**, NOT Patents.
